summary: Defines the Server-Based Certificate Validation Protocol (SCVP), which lets a client ask a server to build and validate a certificate path for it. The server applies a validation policy that includes trust anchors, including checks such as revocation. This can make client software simpler.

plainLanguage.summary: Before an application accepts a certificate, it has to check that the certificate really comes from the organisation it claims, by following a chain of certificates back to a known starting point. This RFC lets a client ask a server to do that work and report back.

questions: how to delegate certificate validation to a server
what does an scvp validation request contain
subtitle: A protocol that lets a server carry out certificate path building and validation on behalf of a client.

tldr.problem: Checking a certificate means building a chain of certificates back to a trust anchor and testing it, and that work is complex and slow for every application that has to accept certificates.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends the certificate and the checks it wants; the server replies with a status and, optionally, the chain, the public key and the revocation information it found.
tldr.outcome: Clients can either delegate the whole job or only the chain-building part. The cost is that the client must trust the server as much as it would trust its own validation software.

today: RFC 5055 is a Proposed Standard from December 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the SCVP message formats, registers four MIME media types and describes how to carry SCVP over HTTP.

sections.title: Why Hand Certificate Checking to a Server
sections.content:
Certificate validation is complex. If certificate handling is to be widely deployed in a variety of applications and environments, the amount of processing an application needs to perform before it can accept a certificate needs to be reduced. There are a variety of applications that can make use of public key certificates, but these applications are burdened with the overhead of constructing and validating the certification paths. SCVP reduces this overhead for two classes of certificate-using applications.

The first class of applications wants just two things: confirmation that the public key belongs to the identity named in the certificate, and confirmation that the public key can be used for the intended purpose. Such clients can completely delegate certification path construction and validation to the SCVP server. This is often referred to as delegated path validation, or DPV.

The second class of applications can perform certification path validation, but they lack a reliable or efficient method of constructing a valid certification path. Such clients delegate certification path construction to the SCVP server, but not validation of the returned certification path. This is often referred to as delegated path discovery, or DPD.

The primary goals of SCVP are to make it easier to deploy public key infrastructure applications by delegating path discovery and validation processing to a server, and to allow central administration of validation policies within an organization.
sections.plainLanguage: Checking a certificate means finding the chain of certificates that leads back to a certificate the client already trusts, and testing every link. The protocol offers two ways out. A client can hand the whole job to the server, or it can ask the server only to find the chain and do the checking itself.

sections.title: The Request and Response Model
sections.content:
SCVP uses a simple request-response model. The SCVP client creates a request and sends it to the SCVP server, and then the server creates a single response and sends it back to the client. The typical use of SCVP is expected to be over HTTP, but it can also be used with email or any other protocol that can transport digitally signed objects.

SCVP includes two request-response pairs. The primary pair handles certificate validation. The secondary pair is used to determine the list of validation policies and default parameters supported by a specific SCVP server, so that a client can find out in advance what the server will accept.

An SCVP client request to the server must be a single CVRequest item, and when a CVRequest is encapsulated in a MIME body part, the media type application/scvp-cv-request must be used. There are two forms of request: unprotected and protected. A protected request authenticates the client to the server, or provides anonymous client integrity over the request-response pair. The protection is provided by a digital signature or a message authentication code, and in the latter case the MAC key is derived using a key agreement algorithm such as Diffie-Hellman. A server may require all requests to be protected and may discard unprotected ones.

The unprotected request consists of a CVRequest encapsulated in a Cryptographic Message Syntax ContentInfo. The protected request consists of a CVRequest encapsulated in either SignedData or AuthenticatedData, which is itself encapsulated in a ContentInfo. All SCVP clients and servers must support SignedData for signed requests and responses, and should support AuthenticatedData for MAC-protected ones.
sections.plainLanguage: One request, one reply. The request can be left open, or it can be signed or protected with a shared secret so the server knows who is asking. The messages are ASN.1 structures, normally carried in a MIME body part and sent over HTTP.

sections.title: What a Validation Request Contains
sections.content:
The query item specifies one or more certificates that are the subject of the request; the certificates can be either public key certificates or attribute certificates. A query must contain a queriedCerts item, one checks item and one validationPolicy item, and may also contain wantBack, responseFlags, serverContextInfo, validationTime, intermediateCerts, revInfos, producedAt and queryExtensions items.

The queriedCerts item is a sequence of one or more certificates, each of which is either directly included or referenced. When a certificate is referenced, a hash of it is included so that the client and the server both obtain the same certificate when the reference is fetched. The certificate hash is computed over the entire DER-encoded certificate, including the signature.

The checks item describes the checking the client wants done, as a sequence of object identifiers. For each check requested, the server must perform it or return an error. The wantBack item lists what the client wants back beyond the results of those checks, also as object identifiers: the certificate itself, the certification path built, proof of revocation status for each certificate in the path, the public key, a set of certification paths, or the responses the server itself received from other servers.

The responseFlags item lets the client ask for optional features of the response: the full request echoed back, the validation policy parameters spelled out rather than referenced, a protected response, or a cached response. The serverContextInfo item tells the server that additional information from a previous exchange is wanted, which is how a client asks for one certification path at a time. The validationTime item tells the server which date and time the checks should be relative to; it must be a retrospective time, and the default clock skew applied by servers is 10 minutes.
sections.plainLanguage: The request says which certificate is the subject, which checks the client wants, and what extra material the client wants back, such as the chain of certificates or proof that nothing in it has been revoked. It can also ask the server to work from a moment in the past rather than now.

sections.title: Validation Policies and Algorithms
sections.content:
The validationPolicy item defines the validation policy the client wants the server to use. A validation policy specifies the rules and parameters used by the server when validating a certificate. In SCVP, the policy is either fully referenced in the request, so that no additional parameters are necessary, or referenced with additional parameters. A policy must define default values for all parameters necessary for processing a request, and for each parameter it may either allow the client to specify a non-default value or forbid it. If the request conflicts with the policy, the server must return an error response.

A server publishes the references of the validation policies it supports, and the default values for any parameters that may be overridden, so that a client can leave out a parameter it is happy with the default for. The default validation policy corresponds to standard certification path processing with server-chosen values, and its object identifier is id-svp-defaultValPolicy. It must use the basic validation algorithm and has no parameters of its own.

The validationAlg item defines the algorithm the server uses during validation, represented by an object identifier. SCVP defines a basic validation algorithm, which for identity certificates implements the certification path validation algorithm from the PKIX specification, and a name validation algorithm, which adds a check on the name in the certificate. Both must be recognised by servers, and new application-specific algorithms can be defined in other documents.

The remaining policy parameters are the ones defined by PKIX: the initial policy set, the inhibit policy mapping setting, the inhibit anyPolicy setting, the require explicit policy setting, the trust anchors, the key usages, the extended key usages, and any specific key usages the client insists on. A client that sets a policy set other than anyPolicy should also set requireExplicitPolicy, otherwise the server may return an affirmative answer for paths that satisfy none of the requested policies.
sections.plainLanguage: A validation policy is the rulebook the server applies: which certificates it will accept as the starting point, which purposes the key may be used for, and which policies the chain must satisfy. The client names a policy and can override some of its settings. Naming the policy by an identifier keeps the request short.

sections.title: What the Reply Contains
sections.content:
An SCVP server response to the client must be a single CVResponse item, and when it is encapsulated in a MIME body part, the media type application/scvp-cv-response must be used. The CVResponse must contain the cvResponseVersion, serverConfigurationID, producedAt and responseStatus items, and may also contain the respValidationPolicy, requestRef, requestorRef, requestorName, replyObjects, respNonce, serverContextInfo, cvResponseExtensions and requestorText items. The replyObjects item must contain exactly one CertReply item for each certificate requested.

There are a number of forms of response. A success response to a request that has protectResponse set to FALSE should not be protected by the server, and the server must protect all other success responses. An error response to a request made over a protected transport such as TLS should not be protected, while an error response to an authenticated request should be. Where a protected response is required, the server must use SignedData or AuthenticatedData even if the transaction is performed over a protected transport, and if the server is protecting a response to a protected request it must use the same protection mechanism as in the request.

A successful response is one where the server was able to attempt to build a certification path using the referenced or supplied validation policy and could comply with all the requested parameters. If the server cannot validate using the required policy, or the request contains an unsupported option, it must return an error response. Within a CertReply item, the replyStatus gives the status for that individual certificate, while the responseStatus gives the status of the whole request.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply carries one result per certificate asked about, plus the status of the exchange as a whole. The server normally signs or MAC-protects the reply, and it must use the same kind of protection the client used.

sections.title: Status Codes
sections.content:
The responseStatus item gives status information about the request as a whole. Its status codes cover the whole exchange: 0 means the request was fully processed; 1 means the request included some unrecognized non-critical extensions and processing continued by ignoring them; 10 means the server is too busy; 11 means the server decoded the request but there was some other problem with it; 12 means an internal server error occurred; 20 means the structure of the request was wrong; 21 means the version of the request is not supported; 22 means the request included unrecognized items and the server could not continue; 23 means the server could not validate the key used to protect the request; 24 means the signature or MAC did not match the body of the request; 25 means the encoding was not understood; 26 means the request was not authorized; 27 and 28 mean the request included unsupported checks or wantBacks; 29 means the server does not support the protection algorithm the client used; 30 means the server could not validate the client's signature or MAC; 31 means the server could not generate a protected response as requested; 32 means the server has no certificate matching the requested responder name; 40 means the request was previously relayed by the same server; 50 and 51 report an unrecognized validation policy or validation algorithm reference; and 52 to 57 report unsupported request features such as returning the full request or the full policy. Two further codes, 63 and 64, report unrecognized critical extensions in the query or the request.

The replyStatus item gives the status for the individual certificate in a CertReply item: 0 success, 1 a malformed public key certificate, 2 a malformed attribute certificate, 3 historical data for the requested validation time not being available, 4 the referenced certificate not being found or not matching its hash, 5 no certification path could be constructed, 6 the constructed path is not valid under the validation policy, 7 the constructed path is not valid under the policy but a query at a later time may be successful, and 8 all checks were performed successfully but one or more wantBacks could not be satisfied.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two layers of failure. One set of codes says whether the exchange as a whole worked, for example that the request was malformed or the server was too busy. The other set says what happened to one particular certificate, for example that no chain could be built to it.

sections.title: Relaying Between Servers
sections.content:
In some network environments, especially ones that include firewalls, an SCVP server might not be able to obtain all of the information it needs to process a request. The server might be configured to use the services of one or more other SCVP servers to fulfil all requests, and in that case the client is unaware that the first server is using the services of others. The first server acts as a client to another SCVP server.

When one server relays a request to another, an incorrectly configured system of servers can relay the same request back again. Any server that relays requests must implement the conventions described in this section to detect and break loops. A relayed request must include the requestorRef item, built from the value already present plus an additional GeneralName holding an identifier of the relaying server, or, if the request has no requestorRef, one that holds such an identifier. To prevent false loop detection, servers should use identifiers unique within their network of cooperating servers, such as the DNS name of the server or the distinguished name in the server's certificate.

When a server receives a request that contains a requestorRef item, it must check the sequence of names in that item for its own identifier. If it finds its own identifier, it must respond with an error, setting the status code to 40. When a server generates a non-cached response to a relayed request, it must include the requestorRef item from the request in the response.
sections.plainLanguage: A server behind a firewall may not be able to reach the certificates it needs, so it can ask another server and pass the answer back to the client. Each server that forwards a request adds its own name to a list, and a server that sees its own name in the list refuses the request instead of looping.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A client that trusts a server's response for validation of a certificate inherently trusts that server as much as it would trust its own validation software. If an attacker compromises a trusted SCVP server, the attacker can change the validation processing for every client that relies on that server. An SCVP server must therefore be protected at least as well as the trust anchors that it trusts.

Clients must verify that the response matches their original request, that the server performed the appropriate checks for the correct certificates under the requested validation policy for the specified validation time, and that the response includes the requested wantBacks and meets the client's freshness requirements. When the response is used to determine the validity of a certificate, the client must validate the digital signature or MAC on the response, or a man-in-the-middle attack could fool the client into believing modified responses or responses to questions the client did not ask. If the client does not include a requestNonce, or does not check that the nonce in the response matches the value in the request, an attacker can replay previous responses.

If the server does not require some sort of authorization, an attacker can get it to respond to arbitrary requests, which may give information about weaknesses in the server or about the timeliness of its checking. If the server uses serverContextInfo to hold state for a requestor, implementers must take appropriate measures against denial-of-service attacks where an attacker sends many requests at once to force the server to keep a lot of state.

SCVP does not include any confidentiality mechanisms. If confidentiality is needed it can be achieved with a lower-layer security protocol such as TLS. A client not operating on a network with good physical protection must ensure there is integrity over the request-response pair, either by using a protected transport such as TLS or by protecting the request and the response individually with MACs or digital signatures. Historical validation of a certificate returns the known status at the time specified in validationTime; a certificate may have been revoked after that time, so a client may wish to specify a validation time later than the actual time of interest to mitigate this risk.
sections.plainLanguage: Trusting the server means trusting it as much as you would trust your own checking software, so the server has to be protected well. The client must check that the reply really answers its question, that it comes from the server it expected, and that it is fresh, because a stale reply can still be a validly signed one.

viz.caption: THE PARAMETERS A VALIDATION POLICY CAN SET

items.title: userPolicySet
items.text: The set of certificate policies the chain must satisfy.

items.title: inhibitPolicyMapping
items.text: Stops policy mapping between certificates in the chain.

items.title: requireExplicitPolicy
items.text: Requires every certificate in the chain to carry a policy.

items.title: inhibitAnyPolicy
items.text: Stops anyPolicy from satisfying the policy requirement.

items.title: trustAnchors
items.text: The certificates the chain is allowed to start from.

items.title: keyUsages
items.text: The key usage bits the certificate must assert.

items.title: extendedKeyUsages
items.text: The extended key usages the certificate must assert.

items.title: specifiedKeyUsages
items.text: Usages the client insists on, which the certificate extension must contain.
